point_one.role: Use the notification-sound experiment to distinguish visible phone checking from hidden cognitive control: the alert creates an involuntary control demand even when no one reaches for the phone.
point_one.new_listener_takeaway: A person can keep their eyes and hands off the screen yet still spend mental effort suppressing the alert’s pull and re-establishing focus. In other words, “I did not check it” does not mean “it had no cognitive cost.”
point_one.evidence_anchor: F-001–F-003: in the 73-student Navon-letter experiment, notification trials produced slower responses and larger N2 amplitudes than control-sound trials, despite participants not looking at or touching a phone; F-004 describes the 960-trial task.
point_one.why_it_matters: This reframes distraction as more than lost minutes spent reading a message: the interruption can reduce performance through covert control work. For demanding tasks, reducing incoming notification cues may therefore matter more than relying only on willpower after an alert arrives.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the basic headline that notification trials were slower or had larger N2 responses, or retell the full participant and task details. Use those findings only to develop the additional distinction between overt checking and hidden control effort.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not discuss a silent or powered-off phone on the desk, moving the phone to another room, or the broader survey pattern of habitual checking and phone-related anxiety; this point concerns the acute effect of hearing an alert.

point_two.role: Turn the phone-presence experiment into a two-stage account of distraction: the device can consume attention as a standing possibility before any notification or screen display appears.
point_two.new_listener_takeaway: Silencing or powering off a phone is not necessarily equivalent to removing it from the workspace. With no notifications and the phone switched off, students still performed worse when it was on the desk than when it was in another room: attention scores were 99.71 versus 108.95, and processing-speed scores were 98.48 versus 108.57.
point_two.evidence_anchor: F-005–F-007: the 42-student d2-R experiment compared a phone on the desk with the phone absent in another room, while both conditions excluded notifications and used a powered-off phone.
point_two.why_it_matters: The result gives focus management a concrete environmental implication: for deep work, physical distance may address the background readiness to respond that silence alone leaves in place. It also shows that distraction can begin before an alert becomes an event.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the notification-sound mechanism, the N2 explanation, or the Pew findings about morning checking and distress when the phone is absent. Do not merely restate that phone presence lowered scores; make the silence-versus-distance distinction the point’s added value.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not explain the moment-to-moment attentional capture caused by a notification or the hidden control effort required to resist it. This point should remain focused on the no-alert baseline effect and the practical meaning of phone placement.
